slides.title: Writing Large Numbers in Scientific Notation
slides.note: Post the learning target. Say the 'today' line and nothing else yet.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.sub: On your own. Four minutes. No notes.
slides.note: Q2 and Q4 are the two halves of today: a power of 10 names a place. 10⁶ is a million, and the 4 in 4,500,000 sits in the millions place, so 4,500,000 is 4.5 millions — 4.5 × 10⁶. Say that sentence once at the reveal and the lesson is half taught.

slides.title: Warm-Up
slides.note: Reveal. Ask for the band each question came from only if time allows.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note: The exponent is the number of zeros, and it is also the place of the 1: 10³ is one thousand, and the 1 sits in the thousands place. Students fill the last two cells. Then the book's warm-up number: seven quintillion, five hundred quadrillion grains of sand on Earth's beaches, 7,500,000,000,000,000,000 — twenty digits, and nobody wants to copy it twice.

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Definition first, then the two examples. 2,000,000 is 2 millions: 2 × 10⁶. 26,000,000 is 2.6 ten-millions: the 2 is in the ten-millions place, so 2.6 × 10⁷. The rule of thumb — count how many places the decimal point moves — is on the last line, and it agrees with place value every time. Then the constraint, which the state guide names as the first misconception: 20 × 10⁵ equals 2,000,000 but is NOT scientific notation, because 20 is not less than 10.
OFF: 'One nonzero digit in front of the decimal point. That is the whole rule.'

slides.title: Notes
slides.note:
Three cases, one line each. Same power of 10: divide the coefficients. Same coefficient: divide the powers — and 10³ times is one thousand times, not three times, which is the guide's second named misconception. Both different: divide both and multiply the results. The last line is the calculator: 8.4E6 means 8.4 × 10⁶; E is not an error.
OFF: '10³ times larger is a thousand times larger. The exponent is not the answer; the power is.'

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. The book's Florida education-funding figure. Ask which digit goes in front of the decimal point and which place it is in before anyone writes.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.note: The 3 is in the ten-billions place: 10¹⁰. The coefficient keeps every nonzero digit after it — 3.01, not 3.1 and not 3. A board with 3.1 × 10¹⁰ dropped the zero between the 3 and the 1; a board with 3.01 × 10⁹ counted the zeros after the 1 instead of the places the point moved.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: The book's auction painting. Catches 1.15 × 10⁸ (dropped the zero) and 1.105 × 10⁷ (counted the zeros after the 5). 1.105 × 10⁸ is right.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: SPOKEN ONLY. Coefficients differ and powers differ. Ask for the plan — divide both, multiply the results — before anyone touches a calculator.

slides.title: Example 2
slides.note: 8.1 ÷ 5.4 = 1.5 and 10⁸ ÷ 10⁷ = 10. So 15 times. A board with 1.5 stopped at the coefficients; a board with 10 stopped at the powers; a board with 150 wrote 10² for 10⁸ ÷ 10⁷. Confirm in standard form: 810,000,000 ÷ 54,000,000 = 15.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.sub: Same steps, your numbers. Boards up when done.
slides.note: The book's alligators. 1.5 ÷ 2.0 = 0.75 and 10⁶ ÷ 10⁵ = 10, so 7.5 — a case where the coefficient ratio is less than 1 and the answer is still 'times larger'. A board with 0.75 forgot the powers.

slides.title: Your Turn
slides.note: Reveal; name what a wrong board most likely did (see the note above).
